SPEECH OF THE MINISTER OF MILITIA. Mr. BUREAU:
Did the Minister of Militia and Defence make use of the following language on the 7th May instant, at the Hintonburg Orange Hall dedication:-
' He was delighted to be present, and warmly congratulated L. O. L. No. 126 for the splendid structure they had built, and he hoped that this would not be his last visit to it. He went on to recount the history of fhle Orange Order in Canada and the British Empire. Since the Orange Order had been founded it was to be seen how the country has prospered, while before the people had been hewers of wood and drawers of water, but he was glad to say that that period was only a sad memory of the past, because the saying, Britons will not be slaves, stands out too prominently to-day/
' Confederation was founded on the principles of the Orange Order, and he was of the opinion that the Orangemen of the time had a lot to do with it in dividing the country into counties and districts and provinces. Before William of Orange's time the hierarchy ruled, but since his coming the people have ruled, and will continue to rule. The people of to-day lived, as it were, -too much in the past in recounting the deeds of their forefathers. What will the children of to-day have to say about their forefathers unless they get out and make a name for themselves? '
' He laughed to scorn the idea that the rebels of 1837 were patriots and were fighting for a just cause, and vividly portrayed the march of L. O. L. to fight against them. They waited not for the call to arms, but rose as a man to crush the rebels -who were nothing but cranks and crooks who were driven out of their own country and tried to take Canada for the United States/

put to my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) when he introduced the resolution the other day; can he give the House the information which was asked for?

printed, to whom is the contract given and for what quantity?

6,000.	Mr. Bastedo informs me that the total number of bill-boards on which the posters will go is 1,068.
I understand that the department does not only use the fences of private owners but that it will also use the bill-boards which we see along the railway tracks in the fields.

I do not think these people have any of those bill-boards which we see in the fields along the railway. These people have bill-boards of their own

I do not doubt the
ability of this company to produce excellent posters, and I have congratulated the department on their very striking character, but there is a statute which says that any contract over $5,000 requires to be let after calling for public tenders. How did the Postmaster General evade that statute?

We tried advertising

fully into tlie matter and making inquiries from their former patrons as to the success of the poster system, he came to the conclusion that it was worth trying. My hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) will not find any statute binding the post office in a case like this. There is a statute referring to contracts, but this is special work and we have to go to the men who can do the work.

Were efforts made before this contract for lithographing was made to get prices from others?

We, who are in business, have propositions for advertising constantly coming before us. I do not blame . the man who got Mr. Bastedo to adopt his plan; I think he was a pretty good agent. But a business firm solicited for advertising by one of those engaged in this business would not accept the suggestion submitted without hearing from others who carry on advertising business. I do not mean, as suggested by the hon. mem-15 PELLETIER.
ber for Rouville, that tenders should be called for; but Mr. Bastedo could easily have found by writing to other firms what was the beat offer that could be had. Merely because the agent was certain that his people were the only people in the country who could do the work, we should not conclude that that was necessarily the case. There are many firms in this country quite as responsible as those with whom the department has been working, and it is only a reasonable business precaution to consult those who could offer a basis of competition.
Mr. Bastedo tells me, and I agree with him, that these were the best people for the special work to be done-
The Stone people are not the best; they may be very excellent people, but not the best.
What I started to say was that Mr. Bastedo in this matter did what he thought was in the public interest, just as he would do in his own business.
I would not like 'to engage him for such work.
I have found him a .most efficient officer, one who takes great pains and is succeeding very well in his vork, and I place the greatest confidence-
I have not a word to say against his ability.

The hon- gentleman
must remember that we succeeded in having a reduction on the current price of $1,500.
I suppose the hon. minister has heard of the Morgan catalogues, piano catalogues, and he knows the catalogue prices of these things.

I am informed, moreover, that, the newspapers advertising having been discontinued as not giving us a fair return, the head of the branch thought it necessary to go into this new kind of advertising at once.

It would not be orthodox for me to forsake the newspaper advertising. But it all depends on how you do it. An inch or two is no good. To reach the-public you have to take space, a good big contract, and continue it for some time. And the advertising has to be written professionally ; I believe it is an art in itself.
I have handled a gool deal of lithographic work in past years, and I admit that you cannot very well advertise for tenders for such work, there is so much difference in the qualify. The method I pursued was to communicate with certain well-known firms and tell them: We want to put on so-and-so; let me hr/e your designs and prices. I
- MAY 14, 1913
never dealt with any but the very best firms. If my hon. friend the Postmaster General would consult the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) as an election manager, he would find the same thing. That lion, gentleman would say to such firms:	We want to show ourselves in this
light and to show the other fellows in the other light; let us see what your artists can do and give us prices. In that way you have competition both in prices and in design. The Postmaster General and Mr. Bastedo also, will find that there is nothing in the world in which there is such diversity of prices as in lithograph work. You will have two designs placed before you from two good firms, one design for all practical purposes as good as the other to reach the end designed, and yet there will be a difference of perhaps 50 per cent in the prices. If one has ideas of his own, probably he works it out in a different way. He gets a foundation for his design, it may be a photograph, it may be a painting,-something that strikes him as affording a central idea. This he takes to three or four of the lithograph people, and asks them to use this as a main feature and to furnish the necessary embellishment. These are hints I throw out from practical experience of years in this business. Within the next couple of years the department itself may come across some idea in the pictorial line that would be exactly what is needed in its work, something very effective. The patent medicine firms, for instance, do not accept indiscriminately the designs for the covers of their books and pamphlets as offered by the printing company; they select their own designs and let the lithographic company put on the embellishments. To my mind the only businesslike way of doing this is to place before five or six of the best firms the object you have in view and the matter you desire to place before the public, and you thereby have the selection of your own designs and prices.
My hon. friend the Postmaster General said the other day that the postmasters were being supplied with pamphlets or booklets. That is a good idea, so far as it goes, but it struck me that the department might go further by mailing to each elector of Canada a little booklet containing information on the subject. Nothing appeals to a man more readily than something which is mailed direct to him; if the postmasters hand it to him, it is less likely to have the desired effect. The PostmasteT General, in order to reach the electorate on a political matter, would not send the literature to the postmaster and ask him to deliver it; he would mail the matter to the elector direct. I think, therefore, that there is no better way of reaching the electors than by mailing direct to them a booklet
setting forth the benefits and advantages of the annuities system. It is a good Act, and, properly worked out, I think it will bring much benefit to the people. The system has one advantage over all other institutions of its kind in that it gives absolute security with practically no cost to the participants for administration. If it is properly placed before the people-and even this will take time-in a few years a vast amount of business will be done by the department in that regard, not for the benefit of the Government, but for the benefit of the people of the country.

Am I right when I say that there is a statute which compels the minister at the head of any department to call for tenders whenever the contract is over $5,000? My hon. friend the Postmaster General has given to the Stone Company, Limited, a two-years' contract for the printing of large posters involving the sum of about $28,000. Would the Prime Minister tell me how the department can avoid calling for tenders, in the face of the statute? Does the statute affect only the Public Works Department; or does it apply to other departments?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The statute, as I recollect it, applies only to public works, but in practice it is followed out in all the departments.

In the present instance I think my hon. friend the Postmaster General should have called for tenders. As my hon. friend the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) says, the Stone Company is not the only company that can print these posters. I quite admit that the posters are a credit to the department, but we are discussing the principle. When I was in journalistic work, the Montreal Gazette used to execute contracts for the printing of large posters, theatre advertisements, and so on. Why is it that the Post Office Department went to the firm of Stone, Limited-against whom, of course, I have no prejudice whatsoever-and ignored the other lithographing firms in Canada? There are printing and lithographing firms in all the large cities of this Dominion, and the Government, at least in a case of this kind, ought to try to encourage competition. If these booklets are issued in large quantities, will they be printed by the Printing Bureau?
Yes.
For the future I would advise my hon. friend to call for tenders in regard to these large contracts.

When the advertising in the newspapers was dropped because it did not produce the results that were expected, these people came to us with this suggestion-and	hon. gentlemen have

agreed that the poster is a very striking and creditable one. It was the idea of the company; they came to us and offered to do it at the regular price charged to all their customers. Mr. Bastedo did not think that we should take these designs as suggested to us by one company and go with them to another.
That is quite right; there was no necessity for doing that.

I think it is only fair, if a man comes to you with something that suits you, and offers it to you at a reasonable price, that you should get the benefit of it. As I said a moment ago, the information which Mr. Bastedo got with regard to these people, from some of their patrons, was that the work they were doing for them was productive of the most satisfactory results. We got a reduction of $1,500 in the ordinary price, and I think this is as well as anyone could do. There is no law obliging us to ask for tenders in the Post Office Department except for the carrying of mails. It is general to ask for tenders when the general public can compete, but here was a suggestion made by one company and, if the price is fair-and it has not been contended that it is not fair, because we are paying $1,500 less than the regular customers of these people-I think we are doing pretty well.
One would have to know what the customers were paying.

Mr. Bastedo said that it was after considerable pressure by him upon the company that he succeeded in obtaining this reduction, and we considered that we were making a very good bargain indeed. In addition we got these small posters thrown in, which cost us nothing. So that, on the whole, as I have said, hon. gentlemen will see that we have made a very good bargain.
Mr. Chairman, I would like the minister to tell us how much the pamplets cost a thousand.

Those pamphlets are printed at the Printing Bureau. As to* those notices or posters, I have stated a moment ago what they cost. Those notices of small size, as my hon. friend has got a few before him, with the large size posters which can be seen in the streets, will cost $15,000 a year instead of $28,000 which the lecturers used to cost us.
I have given those figures a while ago, and my hon. friend shall find them in ' Hansard.'

When business men require any work of this kind, it is customary for them to give the companies an idea of' Mr. PELLETIER.
what they want, and let them make up the designs, to be afterwards submitted or approval. In that way there are four or five designs to choose from; you do not steal one man's design and give it to another. The fact that these small posters were thrown in shows that the company made enough out of the others to be enabled to do so. These people are not doing business for charity. There are many firms who give fifty per cent or sixty per cent discount off their catalogue prices to all their wholesale customers. I am finding fault not with the price, but with the system that is being employed. It is the principle that is wrong, in my judgment. I think also that you should not make a contract for two years; this is nothing more nor less than an experiment. The hon. minister has said that the newspaper advertising was not a success. As a matter of fact the largest advertisers in this country are those who stick to the principle of advertising in newspapers and magazines. There is nothing so wasteful as these billboards; everybody destroys them. They are destroyed by every boy who goes along the road.
These people have employees at the different points; the posters are regularly inspected, and if destroyed are at once replaced.

I admit that the hon.
minister's intentions are good but these people who are employed to look after the posters will not do the work properly and the bill-boards will in many eases be destroyed. This is a very expensive experiment, and I think the hon. minister should not have entered into a contract for two years without first trying it out for a shorter period.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I would remind the hon. gentleman that some of the largest advertisers use bill-boards very extensively -Penman's, for instance.

I do not know of any firm, other than the hon. gentleman's and Penman's that has had more success with bill-boards than with any newspapers, but I may tell the hon. gentleman that there are just as many people, just as large and larger advertisers as the hon; gentleman and who do a greater business, who advertise only in magazines and newspapers. Of course, it is largely a matter of opinion, but so far as I am personally concerned,
I would not give a straw for the bill-board advertising; I use magazine and newspaper advertising exclusively.

I have a great deal of respect for the opinions of my hon. friend, but the head of the Annuities Branch informs me that, as a result of the billboard

advertising the number of inquiries have increased by sixty-six per cent.
That is probably the result of the newspaper advertising, whicli is just now making itself manifest.
I do not think so.

With regard to what the hon. member for Colchester said, I may say that Stanfield's Unshrinkable does not need any advertising. But, coming back to the statute with regard to contract for more than five years, hon. gentlemen will find in the Revised Statutes, volume 1, page 39, section 36, the following:
Whenever any works are to be executed under the direction of any department of the Government, the minister having charge of such department shall invite tenders by public advertisement for the execution of such works, except in cases:
(a)	of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest; or
(b)	in which from the nature of the work it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department; or,
(c)	where the estimated cost of the work is less than five thousand dollars and it appears to the minister, in view of the nature of the work, that it is not advisable to invite tenders.
2. Whenever in case of any work tenders are required to be invited, the minister having charge of the department concerned shall submit all tenders received therefor to the Governor in Council and the contract for the work shall be awarded under the direction of the Governor in Council.
I am sorry that in the present instance my hon friend has clearly violated the law. This statute does not apply only to public works; it applies to all departments, and the cases in which tenders are not to be invited are clearly set forth. Under the circumstances, I think my hon. friend should cancel the contract and call for tenders.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend has evidently misconstrued the statute, a portion of which reads:
Whenever any works are to be executed under the direction of any deparment of the Government.
This is a work,

speechtext: This is not a 'work' in the sense in which it is evidently used in this statute, and this is the statute with regard to public works.
Yes, but it is a general clause.

I know it is, and it uses this language:	..
Whenever any works are to be executed under the direction of any department of the Government, the minister having charge of such department shall invite tenders by public advertisement for the execution of such works, except in cases:
(a)	of pressing emergency, in which delay would be injurious to the public interest;
That is to say in the case of a work which has to be executed very quickly to avoid destruction or damage to some public property.
(b)	in which, from the nature of the work, it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department; or,
(c)	where the estimated cost of the work is less than five thousand dollars, and it appears to the minister, in view of the nature of the work, that it is not advisable to invite tenders.
Obviously it does not apply to cases of this kind, but as I have already said, even in cases to which it does not apply, the usual practice has been to observe that rule, that is, to call for tenders. In some cases, in fact in all cases where the rule is departed from, so far as the Public Works Department is concerned, it must be departed from under the terms of an Order in Council as provided by the statute.
Was there an Order in Council in the present instance?

speechtext: I am not aware of that, but I do not thipk that advertising is to be regarded as a public work within the meaning of the statute.

Surely we have come down to a somewhat narrow margin if the principle, which my hon. friend from Rou-ville urges, is to obtain. We want to advertise in the newspapers, and this was an advertisement, nothing more or less. Who has ever thought of asking for tenders for advertisements? We advertise for tenders in the different newspapers, and we pay thousands and thousands of dollars for advertising, but who ever thought of asking for tenders for that advertising. We have ascertained that advertising in this way is productive of the best results. The head of the branch was satisfied that it was in the best interests of the people to advertise in that way, and now we are told it is a 'work' within the meaning of the statute. For a public work plans and specifications are prepared, and the tenders are based on these plans and specifications. That is not the case here. Our object is to try and make known to the public at large that this statute exists, that it is a law in their interests, and we take this means of letting them know. Surely it cannot be called a 'work' in the sense of the statute.

You cannot popularize the annuities system in Canada without advertisement any more than you can send letters through the post office without affixing a stamp to them. - You have to print the stamps. How did we proceed in 1897 in connection with the contract with a firm in Montreal for the printing of Dominion bank notes and post office stamps? We advertised, and, by advertising, we obtained a very large reduction by the competitive system. Surely my hon. friend is too much ot a business man to dispute this point, that whether or not the department has to advertise to popularize the annuities system, the posters are a work auxiliary to the system, and is part of the equipment of the system.
Is it a contract?

Certainly it is a contract. To get the work done in the cheapest way possible, he must call for competition, he must ask the various lithographic 'firms in the country to state their prices. Has he invited any such tenders? He says he has not. He has confined himself to the Stone Company Limited, in Toronto, when I dare say there are in Canada, from Halifax to Vancouver, at least twenty lithographic firms. I do not say that the price is excessive-

The contract is not
with the Stone Company; it is with the E. L. Ruddy Company, Toronto.

You have the bill
boards, and the posters which cover the bill boards. You have the picture which was exhibited to the House a few moments ago, ahd you have large bills on the street. Surely my hon. friend will not contend that if he had asked for tenders from fifteen or sixteen firms in Canada he would not have been in a better position to get a cheaper price. -But he has confined himself to one firm. I would like to know the prices of other firms. My hon. friend has not given me the other data which was asked for the other day in regard to the increase or decrease in the business, and the number of annuities taken by postmasters since they were instructed to take them.

It would be interesting to have the opinion of my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain). He was an authority on this subject at one time. I would like to know just what he thinks about awarding contracts without tenders. Even in regard to advertising in newspapers, he went to very great lengths.

This question of the
construction of the statute is somewhat interesting. I have looked at this statute
Mr. PELLETIER.
several times, and it seems to me it is very wide in its application and that it covers a case of this kind. Clearly, it is applicable to every department of the Government. The meaning that ' works * would have in the Department of Railways would be different of course from the construction you would put on ' works ' in regard to the Department of Public Works, and so on. There are different departments. When the word ' work * is interpreted in connection with the Post Office Department, it certainly means such" works as are necessary in that department . Therefore, the word 1 works ' must receive the construction which would naturally be put upon it in the particular department to which it refers. In this case the Postmaster General, through his officer, gets an idea. The carrying out of that idea requires the making of a map. It is called an advertisement, but it is really a map. It requires the same kind of paper as a map, and has to be designed and engraved in the same way. It also requires a certain board on which that map shall be posted. He wants tens of thousands of those maps and boards made. There is no other word in the English language which covers that much work. It is work to be done for the department, it is not advertising. The Post Office Department are undertaking to do their own advertising in a certain way for which they require a certain outfit and that outfit consists of these posters and boards. They want that work done. It is not play, it is not philosophy, it is work that requires the putting together of certain material in a certain way and those who are engaged in that sort of business, I suppose, have a right to be given an opportunity to do that work if they want to do it and to be given an opportunity for putting in a bid for it. The statute says that they shall be given an opportunity except under certain conditions. This work does not come within any of the exceptions. I submit that the law has not been complied with in this case and that the Prime Minister does not fully explain it by saying that this kind of work, or the supplying of this equipment, is not covered by the word ' work.' I would like to ascertain from the hon. Postmaster General the maximum and minimum annuity that can be granted?
The maximum now is $600 and we propose to raise it to $1,000. The minimum annuity is $50.
.What classes of persons are eligible to be annuitants as to age and health conditions?

Any person over the
age of five years. There is no medical examination whatever.

At what age or ages
does the payment of the annuity begin, and what is the amount of the premium payable on the maximum and minimum annuities?

Five years is the
earliest age at which the payment on account of an annuity can begin. The amount depends on the plan on which the annuity has been purchased as to whether it is deferred or immediate.

Take one case: What
would a man fifty years of age pay for the maximum annuity as we will have it when this Bill becomes law?
Fifty-five years of age is the earliest at which the annuity can begin.
If a man began to pay at, say, forty or fifty, what would the amount of the premium be?

A man at the age of
forty, making an annual payment of $57.56 until he is fifty-five, will secure an annuity of $100. Each additional $100 would cost him at the same rate. He may pay his premium quarterly, monthly, or weekly without any additional cost. This is done to facilitate payments by the labouring classes. I would be glad to send the hon. gentleman one of our little booklets which will give him all the information on the subject.

I am asking the questions here not so much for my own information as to give the matter publicity. I understand that the Act is to be changed so .as to make the maximum annuity $1,000. How is that to be paid?
If this Bill passes, instead of getting $600 as the maximum amount, the annuitant will get $1,000 a year, or he will get $250 quarterly.

What does* he pay at
the age of forty in order to secure to himself an annual payment of $1,000?

It depends on the
system that he adopts. If he wants to have the annuity payment begin at fifty-five, it will cost him a certain amount, and if he wants it to begin at sixty it will cost him a different amount. It is based absolutely on the insurance plan except that there is no medical examination and there is no expense to the public for the administration of the fund. It is supported by the Government, and that is an enormous advantage for the man who buys an annuity knows that he has the Government of the country to pay the annuity each year.

How long would a man commencing payments at the age of forty
have to continue these payments before he would get his annuity?
He may have the annuity begin at any age he likes after fifty-five.
Then do the premiums cease?
Yes, immediately the annuity becomes payable the payment ceases.
If the prospective annuitant dies during the time the payments are being made is the money that has been paid in returned to his heirs?
That is entirely a matter of contract between the department and the annuitant.
If he pays an extra premium the amount that he has paid in is repaid?
He can get repayment if he makes a larger payment.

Will the minister state how the rates compare with the rates charged by insurance companies? I have heard that there is not much advantage in getting an annuity from the Government. Of course, we all know that there is an advantage in the security, but is there any advantage in regard to the rates charged?

If you compare the insurance system with our plan for immediate annuities, the insurance companies can compete with us as far as rates are concerned, although none are giving any better rates and most of them are charging more. Mr. Bastedo informs me that he knows of only one company that charges the same rates as we do. For the deferred, our rates are preferable to the rates of all the insurance companies, a fact which can be easily understood, as there is no loading for the expenses, which are paid out of the consolidated revenue fund.

The rates should be
less.
They are less. When this system is well understood the public will appreciate its enormous advantage and will avail themselves of it.

Suppose a man aged
forty contracts for the maximum annuity which he would draw beginning at the age of sixty, and suppose that man would die when he is fifty-eight years old, would his heirs get anything?

It is entirely a matter of contract between the man purchasing the annuity and the department. Under plan A the estate of the deceased who bought the annuity would get all the money back with compound interest at the rate of

three per cent. There are different plans which meet all the possible necessities of the people.

I call the attention of the Prime Minister to the interpretation clause of the statute concerning public works:
Public work or public works mean and include any works or property under the control of the minister.
This section of the statute has general application to the various departments and therefore this poster work comes under the statute, and there is a clear violation of the law in not calling for public tenders.

speechtext: Not only do I not agree with my hon. friend, but I do not think his contention is even arguable. Advertising in a newspaper or by posters such as this is not a contract within the meaning of the statute. My hon. friend takes it for granted it is, and of course he can make a fine argument based on that false premise.

I do not agree
with the interpretation of the law given by the Prime Minister. Suppose it is not a work in the sense referred to, is it good policy to give such a contract without tenders? The Postmaster General advertises for tenders for carrying the mails and I do not see any distinction between these two services as to there being a contract. Are these posters printed by contract?

The thing is done in exactly the same way as if we would go to a newspaper and ask it to insert an advertisement for us. These billboards do not belong to the Government and are not under the King's Printer, but are the property of the company which does the work. Instead of having this advertisement in the columns of a newspaper they publish it on their own billboards and just the same order is given for this advertisement as we would give for an advertisement in a newspaper. Every agreement for the publication of an advertisement in a newspaper is a contract, if you wish to call it so, but it is known as an order for an advertisement.

There is hq written contract, then, between the Ruddy Company and the department; but the hon. gentleman knows that if an order is given in writing or even verbally it is a contract. For example, when the minister sends an order for advertising to La Patrie in Montreal or L'Evenement, it is a contract.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The contention of my
hon. friends would prevent us advertising at all, because when you advertise for tenders that advertisement would be a contract and you could not do that advertising without tender, and so on ad infinitum.
Mr. PELLETIER.

But the object of this advertising is not the same. The first is an advertisement to get the tenders, and when the contract is given for posters by the Postmaster General, that contract is given for a work; the poster is certainly a work of art if nothing else.

Much as I respect the legal acumen of the Prime Minister, I still insist on my interpretation of the statute. This Act, entitled an Act respecting the Public Works of Canada, is divided into two parts. Part I is confined exclusively to the Department of Public Works and the property and under the control of that department. Part II is not limited in its application; and it contains the general clause to which I referred a moment ago:
Whenever any works are to be executed under the directions of any department of the Government tenders shall be invited.
The Postmaster General knows that the Post Office Department could not build a wall, could not even repair a desk; that is the work of the Department of Public Works. When the Postmaster General undertakes to purchase for the annuities branch posters to be put up all over the country to induce people to take out annuities, that is a ' work ' within the meaning of the Act.

I did not purchase
these. I purchased nothing, but simply paid so much to this company to post notices on the billboards, just as I have paid newspapers for space in their advertising columns.

Formerly, we had
agents, and their salaries were voted by Parliament. Now, the Postmaster General has dispensed with the services of agents, and, seeing the need of advertising in the large centres he buys posters for that purpose.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Suppose that instead of doing it that way, the department had employed sandwich men, used very often in England, would these men be ' public works ' under the meaning of the Act ?

The men would not,
but the posters which constitute the ' sandwich ' would be a ' work ' performed under the direction and authority of the Government. And if the ' work ' exceeds the sum of $5,000, under this statute the Government is bound to call for tenders, Now, my right hon. friend has forgotten the immediate past. I remember when he was sitting on this side witn his band of gallant 'followers, and I remember especially the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) how he pounded his desk and thundered against the Liberal Government because of very small things of this kind

that were allowed to be done. I think I can find in the Halifax platform a resolution against any such work as this on the part of the minister. I would like the hon. gentleman to read over again that section. I do not impugn the good faith of anyone, but I say that there has been a violation of the law according to my interpretation of it. The second part, as 1 have shown, is general and is applicable to any department and the works connected with that department.

Yes, provided it is
' work.'

Will the hon. gentleman say that buying stamps is not a ' work ' of the department ? And does not he call for tenders for that ' work '? Does not he call for tenders for the equipment of post offices and for the mail bags ?

We never call for
tenders for advertisements.

I desire to ask
a question with regard to the sandwich men. Take for example: suppose the Government were sending out men with the Nationalist bill carried in front and a Conservative bill at the back, what kind of ' work ' would that be ?

To what extent
are the public taking advantage of this annuities system ?

I am glad the hon.
member has put the question. I have here the complete information, and I am sure it will interesting to the House and to the public.

I think there was a
series of questions to be asked, and the minister might give the committee information in the form of answers to those questions.

I was going to do
that. Applications for annuities have been received from the following classes:
School teachers, married women, minors, clerks, spinsters, civil servants, farmers, trained 'nurses, students, stenographers, merchants, physicians, book-keepers, photographers, accountants, carpenters, shipping clerks, bank clerks, barristers, civil engineers, dress-makers, postmasters, insurance agents, geologists, shoe-makers, domestics, mariners, travellers, dentists, gardeners, music teachers, barbers, tailors, reporters; freight agents, draughtsmen, drug Clerks, excise officers, lithographers, property agents, harness makers, ferrymen, trackmen, chemical1 engineers, librarians, printers, telegraph operators, lumbermen, peddlers, deaconesses, freight checkers, cable operators, port stewards, business managers, station agents, locomotive engineers, electricians, factory
bands, picture framers, florists, miners, North West mounted police, labourers and shantymen.
It will be a good advertisement for the annuities that it should be known that a minister of the Crown has taken annuities. Without giving names, I think members will understand what I mean, and it will be a very good example for the public. I have here information to give in answer to the questions that were to be asked. The first is a question by the leader of the Opposition:
How many persons have purchased annuities to date?-A. 3,163.
And the hon. member for Rouville asks:
What proportion of new annuities have been taken through the agency of the various postmasters?
A. About forty-five per cent of those purchasing during the past year have remitted through the post offices.
That is not bad.

We expect it to be
better when the postmasters understand it better. Other questions from the hon. member for Rouville, with their answers, are as follows:
What are the expectations of those in charge of the work as to the future expansion of the system?
A. As soon as the people appreciate the enormous benefits tto be obtained from an investment in an annuity, it is believed they will take advantage of the system in large numbers.
What means are taken to induce the public to go to the post office for that purpose?
A. In the more important places the billboard posters already referred to instruct the public to inquire at the post office for information. A miniature of this poster, such as I hold in my hand, will be sent to the post offices. The distribution had been commenced but has been delayed in consequence of its having been found that the covering or carton in which the poster was enclosed was not sufficiently strong to stand the pressure of the heavy mail matter going out from the Ottawa post office. The matter is receiving attention, and the distribution will be made at the earliest possible moment. It is believed that this will supply in the smaller places, where nearly every one goes to the post office, the purpose to be supplied in cities and towns by the larger poster, and that it will readily attract attention.
What number of posters have been placed in Canada?
A. 1,068.	.	.
Is the distribution confined to cities? or is it extended to villages and country districts?
A. The distribution covers 132 cities, towns and villages which have an aggregate population of 2,671,840.
The hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) asks the following questions, to which replies are given:

Q. Has there been an increase in the amount of the premium or payments to be made for annuities?-A. No, the rates remain the same as originally established.
Q. Has there been an increase in the instalments corresponding with the total amount of annuity itself?-A. No, the cost is relatively the same whether the purchase is of the minimum annuity or of the maximum, and purchasers are not tied down to any definite plan of payment, but the greatest freedom is afforded them. They will only receive the amount of annuity that they actually pay for.

Has the Postmaster
General arranged that these posters shall be printed in the French language?

My hon. friend will see posters printed in both languages along the streets right here in Ottawa.

On motion of Hon. Martin Burrell (Minister of Agriculture), Bill No. 198. to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)
On section 1-compensation for animals destroyed:
Would the minister give a statement of the difference between this clause and the Act as it stands?

The difference, as I explained to the House the other day, is that we have raised the maximum value oh grade horses from $150 to $200 and raised the maximum valuation on pure breds to $500, two-thirds of which will be paid as compensation.
I see that it is provided that compensation shall be paid on valuations of $60 per head of cattle and $15 for sheep. Is that in the existing Act?
Except for the alterations in the valuation of horses there is no change in existing compensation.
What are the diseases for which cattle and sheep may be slaughtered?

Practically we are not slaughtering any now. The main diseases we are concerned about in sheep is scab and in cattle, anthrax. We are fighting anthrax by immunizing, the injection of a vaccine, and we supply the vaccine.

It does seem to me that the valuation for a hog of $15, of which two-thirds is paid in case an animal Mr. PELLETIER.
is slaughtered, is very low. Ten dollars is no valuation for a hog at the present time. Has the minister considered the value of the hog relatively to other animals?

My hon. friend is speaking of grade animals. All these points have been considered very carefully by the live stock branch and they concluded that the valuation inserted in the Bill will probably meet the case.

I agree with my hon.
friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson). 1 happened to be on the market last Saturday and I saw sucking pigs sold for twelve dollars a pair. You have got to take off your hat now to anything that walks on four legs.

In regard to he valuation of horses has the minister considered the point of making a different provision for stallions in service. Such horses of course are usually of a much higher value than the valuation that is placed here.
Mr, BURRELL:	We hafve considered
that and have raised it from $300 to $500. Very few stallions have been killed, only four last year out of eight hundred. The fact that we pay $500 would be some alleviation and, as a stallion affected with glanders or dourine is of no value to the owner, the present provision probably meets the case.

The reason I urged that the compensation in the case of a stallion affected with dourine should be increased is that the stallion may be used for a year or two after infection. In some cases the disease develops very slowly. An owner perhaps knows that tTiere is something wrong with the animal, but keeps him in service, and in the meantime the disease is disseminated over a very large area of country. My suggestion to the minister that he should increase the compensation on dourine stallions was with the object of encouraging the owners to Teport such animals.

I quite appreciate the
view put forward by my hon. friend from McLeod (Mr. Warnock), but, as I pointed out the other day, we are going very fully into this question of dourine. I think I gave him the figures, and, on the whole, considering the small number of stallions that have been affected, and the fact that we are adopting a test which I hope will be very satisfactory, I think it would be well to leave it, at all events now, and if it should be found advisable to put in an amendment next year, perhaps it could be done.

Without desiring to criticise the minister or the department, this

may be a favourable opportunity of putting on record my own personal view. I would support the minister in making a distinction owing to the extra value of stallions in service. In regard to these valuations for cattle, I did not understand him clearly. Is- compensation for anthrax now paid under the Act?

No, we have not been
paying compensation for anthrax. As a matter of fact, anthrax is practically nonexistent in Canada now. Compensation used to be paid for it, but lately it has been found that, by the injection of a certain vaccine, you can practically immunize the animal. We have been adopting that method lately, and supplying the vaccine if any case of anthrax occurred.

No cattle disease is
scheduled for compensation at the present time?
No.

Because, at the_ present
crisis in connection with cattle, it would seem to me that the valuation in the Bill is perhaps a little low. But of course if it is not in operation, it makes no difference.

On motion of Hon. George H. Perley (acting Minister of Trade and Commerce") Bill No. 192, to amend the Canada Grain Act, was read the second time, and House went into Committee of the Whole thereon. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)

Before we take up consideration of this Bill, I would like to say a few words on the subject of interior terminal elevators. This question has been under very careful consideration for a long time by the Board of Grain Commissioners, by the Department of Trade and Commerce, and by the ministers and members from the western provinces. We all agree that everything possible ought to be done to assist the quick and profitable marketing of our immense grain crop in the Northwest. With the ever-increasing number of immigrants who are coming to this country, and who are chiefly locating in the Northwest, our grain fields are being rapidly enlarged in area, and are extending to the north and west. The consequence is that the total amount of grain produced is increasing from year to year, and it is difficult for us to take care of it promptly and efficiently. Our railway companies have been making every effort to increase their mileage, to provide larger railway yards and terminal facilities, both in the interior and at terminal points, and also to provide an adequate supply of cars and engines. I believe it is sometimes said that little has been done by way of extending our transportation facilities and storage facilities, but I think that if hon. gentlemen will look at the figures of our railway mileage, and elevator capacity, they will find that great efforts have been made to keep up with the production. The elevator capacity at Fort William and Port Arthur last fall was between 27,000,000 and 28,000,000 bushels, and further elevators are now being built there which will increase the capacity by about 12,000,000 bushels. This will go a long way to relieve the difficulties at that point. The Government is thoroughly alive to the urgent necessity of doing everything possible to assist the farmers of the Northwest to market as large a portion of their crop as possible between the time of harvest and the close of the navigation season on the great lakes. Under the Board of Grain 'Commissioners, a contract was let last year for a large elevator at Port Arthur, having a capacity of three and one quarter million bushels, and this will be ready for use next September in time to assist in marketing this year's crojn Last year there was a larger proportion than usual of wet and damaged grain, more than the drying elevators were able to take care



of. At the request of the Board of Gram Commissioners, and after careful consideration, the Government permitted a United States floating drying elevator to come into Port Arthur and Fort William for the purpose of relieving the situation with the result that a very large quantity of this wet and damaged grain was saved to the great 'benefit of Canadian farmers and owners of grain. To provide further storage facilities during the past winter, the Government, last fall, made arrangements by which a large number of American vessels wintered at Fort William and Port Arthur in order that they might be used for the purpose of storing grain and in that way augment the ordinary elevator capacity. The result has been very beneficial. In another way we have endeavoured to relieve the difficulties there. Last fall, by special efforts, we were able to keep the harbours of Port Arthur and Fort William open much longer than usual. This spring the Department of Marine and Fisheries took special steps to break up the ice above Sault Ste-Marie and in that way they started navigation a week or ten days earlier than would have happened otherwise.
In order to give still further relief, especially in the fall of the year when there is great congestion, there is a strong demand for interior terminal elevators. I regret very much that my hon. colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) is not here himself to place this matter before the House. At the request of the hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce and of the Government, the Grain Commissioners devoted a great deal of time and attention to this subject. Some of their conclusions are embodied in their report which was made last January, and which was printed by order of Parliament. I expect that we shall soon have further details and suggestions from the Board of Grain Commissioners because they have lately been making a trip through Alberta and Saskatchewan for the purpose of gathering more information. I expect that the Chairman of the board will be here this afternoon. He is due here now and I have asked him to come to the House as soon as he arrives in order that I may be able, with his assistance, to answer questions which hon. gentlemen may wish to ask. The Government realize that everything possible should be done to assist in marketing the Northwest grain crop and have decided to build as soon as possible a few interior terminal elevators in order that it may be possible to know definitely to what extent they will be used and how great a benefit they will be. These elevators will be built and controlled by the Government through the Board of Grain Commissioners and, as they will be declared terminal points under the Act, there will have to be a regular staff of inspectors at them and all grain will be weighed and inspected in the same way as is done at Port Mr. PERLEY.
Arthur and Fort William. The grain can then be sold on its inspection and, as the owner will get a warehouse receipt for it; this will become immediately negotiable and the owner will be in a position to sell his grain or borrow money on the warehouse receipt. I need hardly say that it is quite evident that this will be of immense advantage to the farmers of the Northwest and especially in the autumn when everything is so congested.
A transfer elevator will have to be built on the Pacific coast so that it will be ready for use by the time that the. Panama canal is. open and also one at the terminus of the Hudson Bay railway in order that we may get the full benefit of the building of that railway and the facilities for transport which it wall afford. This will enable the holders of grain in these interior terminal elevators to ship it by whichever route gives the most satisfaction and the most remunerative results. These interior terminal elevators will have to be equipped with cleaning and drying apparatus, which will no doubt lead to the erection of hospital elevators and, in the case of damaged grain, -will enable a large proportion of the grain to be saved and put into a marketable condition. Besides that, these elevators will provide a further reserve storage capacity which is so much needed in t'he West and will at the same time bring the inspection of grain into closer relation with its production which, I am sure, will .be a great advantage.
I do not think it is necessary that T should go further into the details of this matter. The Government is anxious and ready to assist in every feasible way the marketing of the products of the Northwest so that our people may receive the greatest possible returns for their labours. We believe that the building of these interior elevators will help very much in this direction. Our policy is to provide for a few of them at the present time in order that we may know definitely the effect that they will produce in the hope and expectation that the results will warrant the building of more later on.

I
presume that this important announcement by the hon. acting Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Perley) is made with the view, not only of placing before the House and the country the policy of the Government, but also of eliciting the views of the members who are present and who have heard the announcement. To sum up, giving the Government every credit for good intentions in their proposal to establish interior terminals and to establish government operation of elevators at Hudson bay and at Vancouver; allowing them credit for the building of the terminal elevator to be operated by the Government at Fort William, they are not meeting the demand that was made or fulfilling the promise that was given.
The other branch of the question is this: that no matter whether there are interior terminals or not, no matter whether there is a government-owned elevator at Hudson bay or Vancouver, so far as present indications point, the great bulk of the trade will still be done though the terminals at lake Superior. It may be that the operations of the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company will have the effect of sending trade elsewhere than by the lakes, but assuming that that beneficent company does not get into the position of exercising that control over rates that it hopes to, and that we have the same freedom of navigation on the lakes in future as we have had in the past, the great bulk of our grain, in the ordinary course of events, will go to these terminals at the head of lake Superior. Therefore it is most important that the handling of the grain that goes through these terminals should be on a principle that will secure to the producer the fullest advantage in the handling of the grain. In an ordinary year, when there is damaged grain or when there is a grain blockade, no doubt the interior terminals wall come into play at the expense of the producer; but in the ordinary year, the year of ordinary production and conditions of marketing, it is safe to say that the terminals at the head of lake Superior will still handle the great bulk of the grain directly as they do to-day. And therefore, while I give the Government credit for what it proposes to do, I am pointing out that it is not thereby relieved in any degree from the responsibility of insuring that the terminals at the head of lake Superior shall be conducted so as to preserve the inspected grade of the grain to insure that there are honest weights, and that there is honest dealing at the head of the lakes, let the expense be what it may. It seems to me that the policy now suggested by the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Perley) concerning interior elevators is eminently desirable, but that we should not move in too great a hurry in that direction, but cautiously. Those elevators will give to the farmer the advantage of a shorter haul for cars; in other words, the cars will be released much more quickly and he promptly sent back to the grain field. Further, they will induce the construction of flour milling industries at places where they will be located, because the millers will always have at hand a large supply of grain and of such a quality that they will have all the necessary raw material out of which properly to make their flour. My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has alleged that the interior terminal elevators proposed to be erected will entail an extra cost to the farmer in the transportation of his grain. This may be true and it may not be true. As the western members at all events will know, the great difficulty with which the farmers in the province of Saskatchewan, and in a portion of the province of Alberta especially, have to contend is that of finding storage for their grain at the present time, because of the large quantity which they grow. It is in view of this congested condition that the Government are taking the action they are taking in connection with the erection of interior terminal elevators in these provinces. And, even if it should turn out that it may entail a small extra cost, at all events it will result in giving the farmers of these two provinces the advantage of being able to find places to store their grain, and thereby save it in some form, and it will

enable them to get it to the market at as early a date as possible. In addition to this, these farmers will have the advantage of getting the cleanings and small grain, which will enable them to feed their stock at a lower cost and to greater advantage, which, in turn, will tend to the development and encouragement of mixed farming and the growing of more stock than we have at present in western Canada. This will more than meet the additional cost, if any, that may be entailed.
While I am on my feet, I may say that in my judgment, the interior terminal elevators should be constructed at points where they will be met by the erection of large flour mills that will be of service to the country, and will probably take advantage of having storage facilities erected by the Government, so that they will be able to operate their mills for the whole year if they see fit and are able to do so. I think that, if it can be brought about, it would be of great advantage to the people of western Canada to have their grain milled in the prairie provinces and shipped from these points to the markets of the world.

I would ask the minister if at these points where storage elevators are to be located, there will be a fully equipped inspection similar to that at Calgary and Winnipeg, and whether there will also exist a survey board and provision for a sample market.

There will be weighing and inspection in and out of these elevators exactly as the act provides for terminal elevators. There is no intention at present of supplying a survey board at all the places where we may put interior terminals; the survey board is provided for in the Act and we have not made any provision to change it. I have been asked whether the grain board has advised the building of these interior terminals and I am happy to say we are following the advice of the Board of Grain Commissioners in that matter as we will try to follow it in all important matters in connection with this great subject of handling our western grain. As to Mr. Castle, I wish to say that the department is exceedingly sorry that Mr. Castle saw fit to resign. A recommendation was made by the board in their report last January that an elevator superintendent should be appointed, who would be the executive officer of the hoard, having charge of licensing, bonding, insurance and so forth, and the intention of the minister and of the board was to place Mr. Castle in that position if he had not made up his mind to Mr. BUCHANAN.
resign from the service. This is an extract from a letter written by Mr. T. A. Crerar, president of the Grain Growers' Grain Company:
From what knowledge I have, I think the appointment of Mr. Jones should be an ex* cellent one. As a result of his experience he should bring to the board a wide knowledge of the different phases of the grain business and should make a very valuable addition to your board.

I would not like to make any promise that cannot be carried out. We have not yet got so far as to discuss that. The supplementary estimates have not yet been brought down but I may say I have recommended to my colleagues that

an item should be put in these estimates for this purpose. Until the estimates have passed and become law it would be impossible for us to take even preliminary steps. I can assure my hon. friend that it will be gone on with just as promptly as possible.

I have not had time to
take that matter up with the Board of Grain Commissioners; Dr. Magill only arrived here this afternoon. I did, however, send a copy of ' Hansard ' to the board in order that they might know what was said on the subject and take the matter into consideration.

There are matters in connection with this whieh T think-should be discussed most fully. May I remind the minister that there is specific provision in the Bill for the creation of a survey board at two points and not at other points. If he contemplates establishing an interior terminal elevator at any point other than these two, I should think it would be necessaray to have a survey board at that point in order to have efficient operation; and provision would have to be made in the Act for that survey board.

My hon. friend knows
that there is no survey board at Port Arthur and Fort William at present.

The grain is not inspected there, but at Winnipeg, where the board is situated. However, I do not wish to argue the point, but to bring out the facts. If it was contemplated to establish interior terminals and to have a survey board, provision would have to be made in the Bill. I understand the hon. minister to take the view that even if an -interior terminal should be established it would not be necessary to have a survey board for that particular locality.
I wish to draw the attention of the minister and the committee to the fact that, aside from the merits of the principle of interior terminals, a great deal of the benefit that is to result will depend on the regulations which govern. The reason I make these remarks is that some of the hon. members who have spoken, said-I think the Minister of Public Works has mentioned it-that the establishment of these interior terminals would have in view the settling of a milling industry at these points. Now if this is to be a policy for the benefit of the milling industry let it be so stated; if it is to be a policy for the benefit of the railroads by enabling them to use their
313i
rolling stock more economically, let it be so stated; but if it is to be for the benefit of the farmers, the Administration will have to have that object in view singly and solely. And while it is not necessary, I presume, to provide any legislation, yet it is in -the last degree important that the regulations which shall apply to these interior terminals shall be so framed that the benefits shall not accrue to others rather than the farmers, if this policy is to be for the farmers' benefit.	[DOT]
Why not for both?
If it is for the benefit of the farmer it is properly also for the benefit of the miller and railway company .and everybody else.

The mills being
there will help the farmer.

Precisely, if they come
there on fair terms. But the trouble is that in this wicked world each interest is endeavouring to get a little bit of advantage; so I am taking opportunity at this early stage of the proceedings to point out to the minister that, while this establishment of interior terminals, will, no doubt, give proper advantages to the milling industry at these points, it would be objectionable from my point of view if that should be made a consideration in framing the regulations governing the handling of the grain at these points. My principle is that the producer of the grain is the person who most needs the protection of this Parliament, and by protecting the producer you must benefit every other class of the community. Every class of the community is entitled to such benefit as may be reasonably secured by the improved conditions of the farmer, but it is not entitled to benefit at the expense of the farmer. So, I say, I can easily understand how these interior terminals may be made very much to the advantage of the milling industry, very much to the advantage of the railway companies; but these institutions and organizations will take care of their own interests; it is the business of the Government and of Parliament to see that the farmers get whatever benefit there is by reason of the regulations that are passed with regard to these elevators.
My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works laid some stress on the argument that by the establishment of interior terminals the farmer would be saved from the individual storage of his grain. My hon. friend does not appreciate the situation at all. The establishment of initial elevators will help the farmer in the storage of his own grain, but the establishment of interior terminals would not help the farmer in that particular. If it is desired to give direct help to the farmer in the matter of storage, the way is to increase initial

storage facilities; the interior terminal elevator is to help the transportation of grain, but not the storage so far as the individual farmer is concerned.
Now, if I am not trespassing too much on the time of the House Committee, I would say further to the minister that there is not only the responsibility of the Government in handling the grain at the head of the lakes-though that after all is the big thing in the handling of our grain- but it was contemplated by the Grain Act introduced by the late Government-and the provision still stands in that Act- that there should be quite as efficient supervision of the grain for the preservation of grade at the transfer elevators and through the whole process of transportation between Fort William and Montreal as at Fort William itself. Now, it strikes me as being as important a duty as the Grain Commission have to perform, to take care of the transfer points for the purpose of preventing the undue mixing of grain and thereby the deterioration of the sample as it reaches British markets. I urge upon the Government and upon the board that while their effort towards improving the transportation facilities from the initial elevator to the terminal at Fort William is quite in line with the welfare of the country; yet, as an experiment-and I do not wish to be understood as endorsing this proposition as being a remedy of itself for difficulties now existing-I am willing to see it pass and to give the Government credit for trying that experiment. But let not that lead them from the responsibility of taking care of the preservation of the grade at Fort William, and not only at Fort William but all along the line of shipment to the hold of the vessel in Montreal.

I am sure the board
will give attention to the suggestion of the hon. member for Edmonton. I am glad he approves of the Government making the attempt to solve the problem in connection with the transport of grain in the West, particularly in the fall of the year. I understood him to put a question a short time ago as to whether this policy was put forward by the Government in . any way to assist the milling industry or the railroads. I can assure my hon. friend that the sole and primary object we had in view in suggesting the building of these elevators was to help the grower of grain to get his returns as quickly as posi-sible, and in the most satisfactory manner. It is very likely that milling industries will grow up near these terminal elevators, because the millers will always have an adequate supply of grain, but no condition whatever will be attached to the building of these elevators at any particu-Mr. OLIVER.
lar point. We hope that milling industries will spring up around them, but our main consideration is to assist the grain grower. Nor are we bringing in this policy for the purpose of helping the railroads. The hope we entertain is that the building of these elevators will primarily help the grower of grain, and sec- * ondarily assist the milling industry and the railroads, because the owner of grain will have a better chance to market bis produce in a satisfactory manner.

There seems to be a conflict between .section 1 and section 2. Section 1 amends section 24 and provides that the chief inspector shall have an inspector's certificate, while section 2 refers to section 44 and provides that such chief inspector shall not require a certificate.

The object of the change is this:	The chief inspector must have an
ordinary inspector's certificate, but when he is appointed to the office of chief inspector, which is a business appointment, requiring different qualifications, he is not required to go before the Board of Examiners again for a further certificate.

Does not the minister
recognize that there might be cases where this change might prove very, harmful. For instance, I cannot see anything to prevent the board taking a man who had years before been an inspector but had since left the service of the department, had perhaps engaged in some other occupation so that he was no longer really qualified as an inspector and appointing him chief inspector. Ought not the chief inspector to be subject to a special examination in order that it may be ascertained that he is qualified for the particular work?

The object of the certificate in the first instance is to be sure that the man knows how to grade grain properly. That examination is carried on by a board of examiners as provided in the Act. The chief inspector, when appointed, must have an ordinary inspector's certificate. He must have a great many other qualifications such as business ability and the capacity to manage men. For these qualifications it would seem that the best authority to examine him is the Board of Grain Commissioners, not the Board of Examiners. The Board of Examiners is made up of

gentlemen engaged in the trade in Winnipeg and it hardly seems reasonable that they should be called upon to judge the qualifications of a chief inspector, provided always that he has had an inspector's certificate.
I am still at a loss to see why the change is made.

Under the amended Act, the inspector must still have received an inspector's certificate from the Board of Examiners but he is nit called on to pass an examination as chief inspector before the Board of Examiners. The clause as it reads in the present Act would look as if the Board of Examiners were the proper authority to say whether he was fit in other ways to be chief inspector, which we think should be left entirely to the recommendation of the Grain Commission.

speechtext:
The difficulty arises in
this way. Section 4 provides that chief inspectors, inspectors and deputy inspectors shall be appointed only from among duly qualified persons certified as such by a board of examiners, as hereinafter provided. It was thought that a reasonable intention of that section might be that the person selected must have not only a certificate as inspector, but a certificate also as chief inspector. This merely provides that he need not have any other certificate than an inspector's certificate.

I think that is a very
strained construction to put on the section. When a gentleman is assuming the important duties of chief inspector, it is no, derogatory to his dignity or to the dignity of his office that at that time he should pass a technical examination before a board of examiners in respect to the grading of grain.
As inspector?
That is all that I read in this section, that he must pass an examination as inspector, and I submit it is a strained construction to put upon it.

Sections 44 and 24 have to be read together. Section 44 says:
No person shall be appointed as chief inspector, who has not been examined by and received a certificate of qualification to act as chief inspector.
It is not intended that he should have to get another certificate from the board of
examiners, but simply that he should have-a certificate as inspector.
I can understand thenecessity of amending section 44 as my hon. friend reads it, but I do not see the necessity of amending section 24.

I wouldsuggest that if the meaning is as was suggested by the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce, the section should be put in a different form, so as to provide that each inspector shall receive a certificate as inspector. A lot of this wording could be cut out, I think, if tne minister would take the trouble to redraft the sections, as they are very confusing and will lead to confusion. I quite agree with what has been said by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) and the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely), that at the time an inspector is about to be appointed chief inspector he should pass an examination. If I read the section properly, though it is so confusing that I doubt whether anyone can read it properly, that would be unnecessary. As proposed, the first subsection of section 24 will read as follows:
Chief inspectors, inspectors, and deputy inspectors shall hold office during pleasure, and shall be appointed only from among duly qualified persons certified as such by a board of examiners as hereinafter provided. Surely that makes it perfectly clear.

Certainly he could. II
four men have been working for years as inspectors, the intention is that the board may pick out the business man of the four as chief inspector, and accept the certificate which he had received as inspector.
Suppose he had received that certificate ten years previously.
If he had been working as inspector for the whole ten years, my hon. friend would not object.

He might have been,
and he might not. I can understand men engaged in law or in some other profession objecting to pass a professional examination in later years, but it seems to me that no person who is to act as chief inspector should have any objection to another examination before he is appointed. The

examination he would have to undergo would be of a technical character to'test his capacity to properly inspect grain. That capacity is very apt to be reduced by age. The chief inspector should be as thorough an expert as any man under him.

What has been the practice up to date when a chief inspector has been appointed? If he held an inspector s certificate, has it been the practice to insist that he undergo another examination before a board of examiners ?

Chief inspectors have
been appointed without any special examination whatever, so I am informed.

Then it must have been
contrary to the Act.

I am informed that was
the custom in my hon. friend's time. I am not saying this by way of criticism, because I see the practical difficulty of carrying out these sections, if construed strictly. We have no intention to alter the spirit of the Act at all; the intention is merely to make that particular point clear.

To my mind the amendment as proposed is merely confusing, and not clarifying. If the acting minister would leave section 24 as it stands, and in section 44 strike out the words ' chief inspector ' where they occur the second time in line 4,

Section 44 does not.
Amended as proposed, it distinctly says he does not require an inspector's certificate.

a man might be appointed a deputy inspector, but if he were going to be an inspector, hp would have to have an inspector's certificate. That is exactly what I

Does the minister insist

Would

This Bill has already

As long as we have the

On section 2-section 44 amended; inspector's certificates:

Are the inspectors and

I think that possibly the difficulty will be removed if you adopt this amendment as it is and add to section 44 these words:
No person shall be appointed as chief inspector unless he holds an inspector's certificate.

Very well; I think it
would.

The board of examiners is composed of men who are engaged in the trade, who have expert knowledge with respect to the transaction of their own business and are necessarily absolutely up to date with their information.
