On section 3-section 47 amended; commercial grades:
Would the minister say what the purpose of this section is?

By section 47 of the present Act provision is made for arranging commercial grades. From the reading of the section it would appear that this had to be done every year. This. amendment simply privides that if the changed conditions do not necessitate the commercial grades being altered every year, the grades made in 1912, for example, shall apply to 1913 without necessitating calling the board to re-enact and change the commercial grades.

Is this amendment recom. mended by the Grain Commission? My understanding is that the commercial grades are fixed because of the special conditions applying to the crop of a certain year. There is no possibility of identical climatic conditions occurring two years in succession. Therefore, it goes without saying that commercial grades fixed without regard to the results of special climatic conditions in a certain year cannot in actual fact be applicable to the results of climatic conditions in the fol'owing year. The proposed amendment, with all due deference to whoever suggested it. is, I think, a mistake.

I am informed that there
have been years when the conditions did not alter sufficiently to make it necessary to provide for different commercial grades. In section 47 it seems to have been intended to make it imperative that this board should be cal'ed together every year to make commercial grades. This alteration

is suggested by the Board of Grain Commissioners, as have all other alterations proposed. It would still be within the discretion of the chief inspector and the members of the standards board to call it together every year if it should be considered necessary. The commercial grades will not be carried over from year to year unless it is proper to do so. There is no intention of enforcing commercial grades when they do not apply to the new crop, but if the conditions are the same as in the previous year, would the hon. gentleman think that the grain survey board should be called together to re enact the commercial grades of the year before?

Adequate statutory provision is made for the grades under ordinary climatic conditions!; the special provision for commercial grades is only made, so as to meet extraordinary climatic conditions. I will admit there is a possibility of the results of the climatic conditions of one year being the same as those of the previous year, but anybody who has lived in the West as long as I have will come to the conclusion that there never are two years exactly alike. It is well-known that a bad season there is exceptional, but the weight of evidence is that the contention that the grades may safely be continued from one year to another is not substantially founded. I speak from personal experience in this and I say theTe is nothing that requires to he so carefully guarded as the grade standard; there is nothing that lends itself to serious manipulation so readily, and the introduction of commercial grades, being an absolute necessity under special conditions, it is just as necessary that that requirement should be safeguarded as it is that the statutory grades should be safeguarded. The minister rests upon the judgment of the Board of Grain Commissioners. I do not want to suggest fr a moment anything derogatory to the good judgment of the board-

I am afraid I have not
made myself plain. Section87 provides that this Grain Standards Board may be called together whenever the Chairman of the said board is notified by the chief inspector or five members of the said board that such a course is necessary. Unless it is conceded on all sides that the seasons are the same and that these commercial grades can consequently remain the same, it is within their power to call the board together every year. I am told there have been two years _ that were exactly the same, and this section simply removes the obligation that the members of the board shall be called together every year unless the grain inspector and five members of the board think it is necessary.
Mr. PERLEY.

I will not insist, but I want to be very emphatic on the point that in the grain business the man who produces and who has to sell cannot afford to trust the man who is going to 'buy, and wherever it is possible to give statutory protection it is desirable that that protection should be given. The commercial' grades fixed for a certain year should not be made applicable automatically tn the conditions of the following year.

I would
like to press the same matter as the hon. member for Edmonton has referred to- that it is not wise, on the contrary it is unsafe, to carry over an extraordinary grade from one bad year, or, if you like, one exceptional year, to another. This section is only intended to apply to exceptional and extraordinary years; and, as the hon. member for Edmonton has said, there are very seldom, if ever, two extraordinary years of the same character. The minister claimed that there were two in western experience.
I did not say there were not more than two.

And I did not say the hon. minister did say so. But he said there were two, and if there were two I think that is about as far as we can go. In my experience-and while I am ready to pay all due respect to the commission, I do not believe that they know one bit more about, this subject than the farmer who has been farming for the last thirty years, and I doubt very much if they know as much- I have never found two extraordinary years, one after another for which the same samples should be used. How are we going to find out what these extraordinary grades should be? There is only one way to find that. You cannot find it by newspaper reports. The only way is to get the board together and have them examine samples from all over and find out what grades these should be. There is no use in -stating that in an extraordinary year it is safe to go on without a board meeting. It would be utterly unsafe and unwise. The effect of this section might be in the m'inds of officials that it would be safe to go on without a board meeting. But it is unsafe, and the minister would be well advised to drop this section.

I do not want to insist
on the section if it is unwise. I suppose the hon. member himself knows what happened. The board was not called together one year, and section 87 was not put in force. Neither the chief inspector nor any five members of the board saw any necessity for calling the board together. But that year, as there had been no meeting, it was questionable whether the grades, which were being inspected the same way as the previous year, were legal-whether the

buyer in England could be forced to take them. All we want to do is to provide that under these circumstances the old grades shall be legal. Just as in the case of a board of directors, it may be provided that there shall be an election every year, but if there is no election the existing directors hold office until successors are appointed.

With all due respect to the board, who did not call themselves together, I think they were wrong and were taking too much upon themselves. I think the legislation should be in such shape that they must be called together.

I would suggest to the
acting minister that the word ' special ' should be inserted before the word ' grade.' Making it read:
3. The special grades selected under subsection 1 of this section shall be the commercial grades until changed.
Hon. members will see that section 47 provides:
If a considerable portion of the crop of wheat dr any other grain for any one year in any division has any marked characteristics which exclude it, to the prejudice of the producer, from the grade to which it otherwise belongs, special grades may be established, therefore in the manner hereinafter provided, and shall be called and known as commercial grades.
The grades under discussion are special grades, as covered by this section 47.

Our objection is the
same. If there are special grades we claim they should be provided each year on the conditions of that year. Just for the purpose of emphasizing the position- the minister will understand that the producing country is about eight hundred miles in length by some four hundred in width at one point; that the conditions vary greatly throughout that territory; and that the conditions which prevailed in a certain year in one part of the country do not prevail in that part of the country in another year but may prevail in some other part. It might be assumed on the opening of the market in the new season that the conditions were the same in a given part of the country because they were the same in some other part, whereas the conditions would be entirely different in the part first referred to. I maintain that the only safe way is to provide for a re-examination every year. That is the only protection the producer has, and the year in which the provisions of section 47 are called into play is the year when the unfortunate producer wants all the protection the law can give him.
There is no intention by this clause to prevent the board from meeting every year.

We want to make
them meet.

This part of the Act is
as it has been for years, and as it was administered by hon. gentlemen opposite. I am not criticising it, but only saying that this is nothing new. In one of the years some time ago during the administration of hon. gentlemen opposite, no board was called together. There are thirty-five or forty members of this Grain Standards Board, but in that year there were not even five who thought it necessary to call the board together. But when they failed to have a meeting there was a question as to whether these grades were good legal grades to tender to the buyer. We only want to do -away with any uncertainty. Any five members of the board can call it together, and it is after samples of the crop come in that they decide about getting together to make commercial grades. I think the horn, member will find that it will work out all right. The hon. member for Brandon suggests the insertion of the word ' special ' before the word " grades ' in the second line of subsection 3. I think that would make it plainer. I merely wish to assure hon. gentlemen that there is no intention of suggesting to the board that they shall not get together, but only to make provision in case for some reason they do not meet.

The fact that the board
failed to do its duty some years ago under the late Administration has no bearing upon the present case. Since that time, I presume because of the fact that under that system there were occasions when everything was not done as it should have been, it has been the mind of Parliament, and of the late Government, to appoint a board of grain commissioners and confer upon them extraordinary power and authority. If there is not in any enactment in regard to this matter a provision that the board shall meet when it is required to meet, certainly the Act should be amended so that this provision shall be included.
My hon. friend is wrong; they did not fail to do their duty.

I understood my hon.

On section 6-section 109 of the Act repealed :

Section 109 of the Act refers to corn shipped from the United States through Canada for export, and section 108 and following sections refer to United States grain. It is provided in section 110:
That standard samples for grain of United States production may be established yearly by the grain survey board of any division or district, and shall be known as the standards for United States grain of that division or district.
This under the law has regard to ail kinds of grain except corn. Section 109 establishes for corn from the United States the same standards that are provided in section 105 for Canadian corn and provides for a moisture test. On section 1-salary of Chief Commissioner :
Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM: There is one thing in reference to this first clause to which I would like to call attention. I am not objecting to the increase of salary to the Chief Commissioner. I belong to the class who think that, if we are to get the proper men to do work of this magnitude, we have to pay them a good salary. My own opinion concerning the present Chairman is that he is a first-class man. I do not think that he was appointed for any political reasons, for I have known him for years, and I do not know if he is a Grit or a Tory. I know he is a man of ability who will do his work well. The point to which I desire to call attention is one wnich also came under my notice when 1 was Minister of Railways. We occasionally find that when a decision is given by this Board the press come out with a claim that it is a party victory, or something of that kind. Now, the poorest service that can be done, either to the members of the Board, or to the country, is for the party press, on either side of politics, to deal with the decisions of the board along that line. I speak advisedly, because, during my regime, I talked to one or two newspaper men who were inclined to do that sort of thing, and pointed out that they had no more right to claim that a finding given by the Board of Railway Commissioners was a party triumph, than to say that a judgment of the Supreme Court was. I want to urge upon the press that they are not doing the Government, or the people, or the Chairman of the board any good service in dealing with the board's findings in that way. This board is a court in a way. It is a court which has to give speedy findings and speedy justice with the minimum of red tape, to all classes of the community, and we should endeavour to keep it as such. I say this because there is an inclination in certain quarters to introduce red tape. I think that at the present time the board is doing good work, and I desire to say a word in favour of the present Chairman, because I think he is filling his position well. My object is to call the attention, not so much of the House, as of the press, to the undesir-

ability of assuming that this board is doing party service, no matter which Government is in power. This board is as high above party as the judge on the Bench, and ought to be so considered if the people are to continue to have confidence in it. One can see at a glance how the board might feel a little timid in giving their judgments if a different idea were to prevail. I have observed that the press has adopted this attitude on one or two occasions during the present Government's regime just as it did when the late Government were in power. It is an injustice to the board, and it is not calculated to do service to the public.

I entirely
appreciate the statement which my hon. friend has been good enough to make, and, might I add, that we give full credit to hon. gentlemen opposite for the formation of the Railway Commission of Canada. In addition to that, I want to say that, on this side of the House, we have always appreciated, as the country has, the men who have been selected since the creation of the Railway Commission to fill the important position of chairman of that body. When it was our misfortune, and the misfortune of the Canadian people to lose the valuable services of Mr. Judge Mabee, who had won in the hearts and affections of the Canadian people a place seldom occupied by any public man in the public service, and the responsibility rested upon the present Government to select a successor to Judge Mabee, I can assure my hon. friends opposite that, since we came into power, we have had few tasks that were more difficult to fulfil than that of finding some individual to fill the place made vacant by the death of Judge Mabee. I appreciate the statement of my hon. friend, for I can assure him that the question of politics, or of anything connected with it, was not considered in regard to the selection of a successor to J udge Mabee. I do not know, nor have I ever heard, what the politics of the present Chairman of the Railway Board are, but I did know, from what I had learned of his ability and qualifications before he was selected, that he was a likely man for the position, and I am glad to know now that, during the time he has filled that position, he has done so with credit to himself, and,
I believe, to the eminent satisfaction of the people of this country. I certainly endorse every word that has been said by my hon. friend f'om South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) that it is a most unfortunate condition that any section of the nress, on either side of politics, should undertake to question the judgments of the Railway Commission, because I think the members of that board, one and all, from the first day thev were appointed, have invariable
' Mr. GRAHAM.
been above any question or consideration of political influence, on one side or the other. For my part, and I am sure I voice the sentiments of members on this side of the House, as well as that of members on the other side, I hope the day is far distant when that board will lose its weight and influence in this country by reason of any attacks that may be made upon its members by the press on either side of politics. On section 2-section 168 amended; alteration of railway, or change of divisional points, &c.; compensation to employees:

Mr. Chairman, I am
quite free to admit that I am in most hearty accord with the proposal that my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) has seen fit to bring before the House as regards compensation for railway employees whom the companies may see fit to move from a divisional point on their line to another location. I was pleased indeed the other day to see the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) bring this matter forward and to hear him intimate that we would have his support for any measure of this nature. All I regret is that the hon. gentleman did not experience that change of heart some little time ago, for if he had done so possibly the town which I have the honour to represent now would

not be placed in the unfortunate predicament in which it finds itself in consequence of the fact that the Grand Trunk Eailway Company are threatening to move their divisional point from Brockville to Prescott. Brockville has been a divisional point of the Grand Trunk railway for fifty-seven and a half years, but in the wisdom of some of the higher officials of the company, they now purpose moving it twelve miles east to Prescott, which is causing a great deal of dissatisfaction among the employees of the company ans also on the part of The merchants and business men of Brockville. It is no wonder that it is causing great dissatisfaction. Some of these men, by industry and economy, have managed to secure for themselves and families, comfortable little homes. In that town which I have the honour to represent, there is $100,000 worth of assessable property owned by Grand Trunk railway employees. You can quite readily understand what will be the result if the proposed change takes place, which change is solely in the interest of the company.
The town of Prescott has seen fit to offer some very large concessions to this company to change their divisional point. These railway employees, to hold their positions, will be compelled to move. Many of them have been residents of our town for thirty years. They have helped to make the town what it is to-day, namely, one of the finest little towns that there is in the Dominion of Canada. We are very loath indeed, to lose these railway employees, because amongst them are some of our very best citizens. They have been foremost in every endeavour that has been put forth to make Brockville the fine town it is and to enable it to hold the high position which it holds to-day. These people are most comfortably situated there, they have every possible advantage that they have in a city like Ottawa or Toronto, outside of a street car system. We have the very best schools that can be provided, an excellent collegiate institute, a fine separate school, very beautiful churches, and two of the best managed hospitals in Canada, good cement sidewalks and pavements, a first-class, up-to-date theatre, a first-class system of sewerage, water-works, gas plant, light plant, parks and all the other advantages which are found in the larger cities; not to mention the fact that Brockville is situated on the beautiful St. Lawrence and at the foot of the Thousand Islands. When you take into consideration that these people must give up all those comforts and advantages, it is a most serious question for them, and I must congratulate the minister upon his introduction of this change in the Eailway Act providing that these men shall receive
some compensation for being compelled to deny themselves all the privileges which they now enjoy. My hon. friend the Minister of Eailways and Canals lhas only held the position which he now occupies for eighteen months, but he has had time to . give this matter his serious consideration and I am quite prepared to agree with the President of the Board of Trade of the city of Halifax in stating that in the person of the present . Minister of Eailways and Canals the railway interests of the country will be most judiciously handled. I extend to him my most hearty congratulations upon his action in proposing to Parliament that some compensation should be afforded to railway employees under circumstances such as I have described. The experience of the railway men at York has been very unsatisfactory. What do we find at Carleton Place, where men have struggled for many years to obtain a home? To-day you can buy out their properties at a discount of from thirty to forty per cent on first cost. That is the unfortunate predicament in which these men are placed. If this divisional point is removed from Brockville it means that the railway employees who are compelled to sell their homes will suffer severe loss.
I referred a moment ago to concessions offered by the town of Prescott to the Grand Trunk railway to remove their shops. I would ask you to consider for a moment who is going to pay the cost of the concessions? It is not only the people who are residing there at the present time but the people who go to make their homes there in the future. These men who move from Brockville have already contributed their share, they enjoy all the facilities which they have helped to provide and it is a great injustice to them to ask them, contrary to their will, to pick up their possessions and move to a town which does not offer them nearly the same advantages as they have in their own town at the present time.
These big corporations that we have in this country should not receive all the consideration that we have to bestow. I think the railway employees who have served the corporations for a long period of time should most certainly receive some of the consideration that the Government is prepared to offer to the labour interests of the country. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, what calling in life is there to-day like the railway service in which a man can work so long and lose the results of his industry and devotion to duty in a moment, and by one mistake may prove fatal to his future prospects. I have known men who worked for twenty-five or thirty-five years and who, through one little mistake, just one slight error of judgment, have lost their situations, have lost their reputations and

have been thrown out upon the world at a time of life when they were little able to adapt themselves to new conditions. The life of a railway employee or a trainman is none too good at any time. Let us look back and see what has occurred on the main line of the Grand Trunk railway between Montreal and Toronto during the last year. How many of those good, noble fellows have gone out into the darkness of the night from their wives and families and have never returned? I have heard people say that railway men are the best paid in the world, but I have had some experience in working upon railways myself and I can say that they earn every dollar that they are paid, and some dollars that they are never paid. I appreciate the fact that the Minister of Railways is taking these matters into his consideration. I most heartily support this clause of the Bill which offers to these railway men some consideration for the loss they may experience. In my constituency there are possibly one hundred men who are deeply interested in the removal of the Grand Trunk terminal and they are much dissatisfied at the thought of leaving their present homes. If it is thought fit by the company to remove these men for the benefit of the company and for the benefit of the company alone, then in justice the men should be compensated. A railway employee who has a grown up family will possibly have four of his children working in some of the many hives of industry in Brockville, and he must either take his children out of employment when the terminal is changed or leave them behind. That is hardly fair play to a man who has been among the best and most respected citizens of Brockville, and if the company is going to receive concessions from the town it is to move its terminal to, it is only fair play that in turn the men should receive some compensation from the company. I most heartily support the Bill.

I will not follow my hon. friend (Mr. Webster) in his criticism of my action or my inaction as he no doubt meant to call it. The situation at Brockville is the growth of the last few months; it was not in contemplation when I was Minister of Railways; it had never been dreamt of and no suggestion of the kind had been made then.

I have heard of it for
the last five years.

I have not heard of it
and I was in close touch with railway affairs when I was minister. I might perhaps retaliate and say that if conditions had not changed in Brockville it would never have been heard of, but I do not wish to retaliate.
Mr. WEBSTER,
You could have exercised your authority.

It was not needed that I
should exercise any authority at that time. However, this is too big a question to bring it down to a local issue, and it is immaterial to the railway men who does it so long as it is done. If we can get a scheme worked out under which the railway men who are placed at a disadvantage when terminals are moved, shall be compensated by the railway companies, then no matter who brings about that desirable condition and no matter who claims credit for it or wants to claim credit for it, I suppose the railway men are not very much concerned so long as they are treated justly. I pointed out some weeks ago here, it is not only the town of Brockville that is affected, but there are Carleton Place and one or two other places on the Canadian Pacific railway as well as some points in the West at which similar conditions prevail. As the country grows and trade expands, there may be reasons why railway companies should move their terminals, but if these reasons are good the companies ought be able to maintain their case before the Board of Railway Commissioners, and they should then be obliged to pay the cost including any loss that may be incurred by the men. I agree with my hon. friend from Brockville (Mr. Webster) as to the losses in many ways, not to speak of the deprivation of old time surroundings which railway employees experience when terminals are changed. I have been criticised by the press of Prescott for introducing my amendment, but I can assure the Minister of Customs I was not trying to get a drive at Prescott; I was trying to do justice to the railway men at the various points at which such a change is or may hereafter be contemplated. The fact that this Bill becomes law will not stop a railway company from moving its terminal if it can make out a good case for doing so, and ;if it does it should bear the expenses, whatever they are, including the loss to the men. I would suggest to the Government that the same rule should be followed on the Government railways wherever men a change is made, and I have no doubt the Government will do so, following the principle laid down in this Bill. I approve of the Bill now introduced by the Minister of Railways, but I would not like to admit that it is as good as my own Bill and I will point out why. The Bill introduced by the minister makes it arbitrary that the board shall say what the loss is to the men, whereas my Bill introduced leaves it optional for the men and the company to come to an agreement without going to the board, and the intervention of the board would only be invoked in case of difference.
This Bill does not prevent that.

If the company should prove a little stiff it -would prevent it. The Bill I introduced said that in case of disagreement between the men and the company the board should fix compensation, but this Bill says that in case of the removal of a divisional point the company shall compensate its employees as the board thinks proper.
Under this Bill the board would have to be asked to interfere1.

No, the company goes
to the board and asks, not only permission to move the terminal but to fix the amount of loss to the employees. Under my Bill the employees could go to the company privately and perhaps they could make a better arrangement with the company than they could obtain from the board.
There is nothing to prevent that in this Bill.
Except that the company would make an application direct to the board and the employees would have no redress.

But if they agree there
would be no appeal to the board.

My hon. friend does
not appreciate my point. Under my Bill it was left open to the company and the employees to agree and the board could say they would not interfere in the case until the parties failed to agree, but in the Bill submitted the company can go at once to the board and ask for its decision.

That helps the
weaker side.

Pardon me, I think it
helps the stronger side. These men want to remain in the employment of the company and they may be old employees who might get better treatment for special causes. Under my Bill, the company could privately make an arrangement with its employees, and the board would not interfere, but under this Bill the company is in a position to appeal to the board to give a decision without trying to come to an agreement with the men. If I were a railway employee, I would prefer to be free to discuss the matter with the company and try to come to an agreement before being obliged to appeal to the board.

Suppose a railway
company makes application for a change of terminal and they state they have agreed with their men, then, under this Bill, the Railway Board could say: that is all right; we are glad you have relieved
us of the responsibility of deciding that question.

Yes, but the company
is not likely to do that when the law states it is part of the duty of the Railway Board to determine the amount of the loss. For example, in fixing the price of light or electrical energy the statute says that in case there is a disagreement between the purchaser of the electrical energy and the producer, then only shall the board be asked to settle it. It is left open for
an	agreement to	be arrived	at	before	the	board	is appealed	to	atall.	That	would	have the effect,	it
seems to me, of putting it in the statute that they are supposed to come to an *agreement, and if they cannot, then they come to the board. It leaves the final court open, but, with the suggestion that they are expected to come to an arrangement. If I were an employee, I would prefer that; I think the employee would fare a good deal better with a settlement, as a rule, than with the matter taken to the board direct and made subject to order in the first place.

It seems to me that the hon. gentleman does not give credit to the company for the intelligence which is possessed by most companies that manage railways. The company would naturally try to arrange the amount of compensation with the men themselves, so that there might not be an arbitrary decision but a chance to get together and argue the question back and forth. If they could get an arrangement, it would be more satisfactory than to have the matter settled arbitrarily by the Board of Railway Commissioners. There can be no question but the company would try to come to an agreement. Why? Because, in the very nature of things they would prejudice their case with the Railway Commissioners if they had made no effort in the first place to make a satisfactory arrangement with their men. So, it seems to me to be better to leave it as it stands rather than to change it as proposed by the hon. member.

My hon. friend agrees
with me exactly. But it is under the amendment I propose that the company would prejudice their case before the board if they had not tried to make an arrangement.

They would, in any
case.

Under the Bill as proposed, they would be merely standing on their rights, for the Bill does not suggest that they should come to an agreement. But I think it will be in the best interests not only of the men but of the company

that they should first try to come to an agreement.

I understand the hon.
gentleman proposes to strike out the section and substitute his own.
No.
Only making a suggestion.

I think two or three
words would fix it. My suggestion is that it shall read:
It shall be made a term of every such order that the railway company obtaining the same shall pay all losses sustained by its employees who may be obliged to change their place of residence from one municipality to another by reason of the change of any such terminal or divisional points.
Then, I add this other clause:
In ease the company and its employees do not agree upon the amount of such loss, the hoard will determine the amount thereof.
The only difference between the two practically is that I make it part of the statute that in case they do not agree the board shall decide. The Bill of the Government provides that the board shall decide without any other proviso. It might [DOT]work out as my hon. friend says, but I submit as a practical matter that mine suggests to the company and the employees that they should endeavour to come to an agreement before referring to the hoard, and that this will promote and facilitate an arrangement. Practically it is a direction of the statute that they shall come to an agreement before they appeal to the hoard. The Government Bill provides that the hoard shall make the order, giving consent to the removal, and at the same time stating the amount of the loss. That would be a quicker way for the company, I suppose, but I think the employees in that case would not have as good an opportunity as through a private negotiation with the company. I would point out to the hon. member for South Renfrew what I think is a misapprehension on his part as to the effect of the Bill introduced by the Government. It has a merit which, I think, he does not quite see. In my advocacy of this matter I seek the same thing that the hon. gentleman seeks. But I would like to point out wherein the Bill introduced by th: minister is best for the men concerned. The Bill as introduced does not say that the board shall only fix the amount of loss. It is a wiser provision than that. It says that compensation shall be as directed by Mr. GRAHAM.
the board which is a much better and wiser legislation than the board undertaking to go to Brockville, or Winnipeg or anywhere else, and acting as land valuators to fix the price of each house affected and the amount of loss upon it through the removal.
Read that section.

The minister's Bill
reads:
-and where a change is made in the location of a terminal or divisional point the company shall compensate its employees as the board deems proper for any financial loss caused to them by change of residence necessitated thereby.
That is not limited to fixing the amount. It also gives the 'board power to direct the manner in which the compensation to be paid shall be ascertained. The board could say: Go to the county judge, or to some other arbitrator, to settle the damages and then they would make an order, just as in the case of extraordinary expropriations.

Does the hon. member
think that that proves exactly what I say -the employee would not be in as good a position if the county judge could be appointed-

The hon. gentleman is -I do not say wilfully-interfering with my argument; I will come to that. I am talking of the proposition of the minister's Bill, and it strikes me as better than the hon. gentleman's. His proposal would require those men and the company to agree as to each individual's damages before any application could be made to the board to change the terminal which might be absolutely necessary in the interests of transportation in the country. portation facilities or the business of the railway company requiring the removal of the terminal, and the individual having an order from the board as to the manner in which he is to prove his damages, goes to the tribunal named by the board and proves his damages in a much cheaper and less troublesome way than he could by having the board determine each individual case before they make the order. I only rise to express myself as being in accord with the views presented to the committee by the previous speakers. The water and electric	power	of	that town	areowned by the municipality, and if they should	happen to	move the	terminal away	from	our town at	anytime in the near future, it would be a great loss to	the	revenue of	the
municipality. On the other hand, the company has always had a certain weapon to hold over the heads of the men in the municipal council. Whenever it was proposed to make an agreement for the supply of water or electricity, the railway would say that if the municipality did not concede to their suggestions, as made by their officials, they would move the divisional point at once to one of the neighbouring towns. I myself have been at council meetings during the course of which such suggestions have been made. I think the clause inserted in this Bill will have the tendency of restraining the company from being so anxious to remove their terminals as readily as if it were not a distinct loss to the company, and thus avoid a serious injustice to all employees.
With reference to what the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), has said as to the company being more favoured than the men, I must say that I cannot agree with him.

I did not desire to convey that impression.
Mr. . COCHRANE:	Suppose you had a
company that was wholly unfair, and took absolutely no interest in the men, it is quite reasonable to assume that they might bring a good deal of pressure to bear on the men, and might say you shall do so and so; you shall take so much. I thought it would be fair to both parties to provide that the railway company should be the one to settle. I have sufficient confidence in tne Railway Board to believe that both parties shall receive fair treatment at their hands, and I think this legislation will be in the interests of the men as well as of the railway company.

I did not mean to reflect on the companies at all. If this provision were not in the Act, the general practice would be for the men and the company to get together; the men would agree with the company as well as the company with the men. The men can always go to the board if they cannot agree, the board is there to protect them. I have had some conversation with railway men with regard to the matter of leaving it quite open to the men to suggest to the company that a settlement might be effected without going to the board. They seemed to be rather inclined to think that they would prefer to have it suggested by the statute that the matter might be settled without going to the trouble of applying to the board. As to the remarks of the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) I do not think the Minister of Railways has his idea in mind at all; the object is to get rid of all this red tape in connection with the payment of compensation. I think the idea of the minister was to hand the matter to the board to settle. If he had thought for a moment of providing under his Act that the matter should be handed to a judge to settle, I do not think the minister would have introduced his Bill, because that would still involve all the roundabout methods which the employees are certainly so desirous of avoiding. It might as well be subject to the ordinary arbitration Act as to be done in that way. It has been thought advisable to extend the authority of the board to say that the terminals shall not be moved without their approval. That being the case, everything incident to that removal should come under authority and control of the board, and one of the things incident to that is the loss sustained by the employees. If anything, I would be inclined to stand by the idea of the minister rather than that of the hon. member for



Lincoln, in order to avoid getting the employees into trouble.

I do not think the
hon. member for South Renfrew yet understands either the minister's Bill or what I tried to say. inis Bill of the minister says that the company shall not remove these terminals unless the company compensates the men in the manner directed by the Board. The matter does not require any arbitration; it requires simply that the board shall stipulate in what manner the men shall be compensated. That does not stop the board from saying they shall send their officials down there to look into the matter as they would look into the question of level crossings. The hon. member for South Renfrew is continually talking about his great faith in this board, but I believe he is afraid of them.
No.

He should show his faith in this board; I am showing mine by saying I will trust them to see that the men get their compensation in the cheapest and most satisfactory way. We all have faith that the board will do this. The minister's Bill says that, but the Bill of the hon. member for South Renfrew does not. It says that these men must go through the form of agreeing with the companies, and only when they fail to agree shall the board be allowed to intervene. The poor man-I use the word not in a disrespectful way

the poor man has got to try to agree with the company, and is obliged to enter into an argument and controversy with them about land values and everything else before the authority of the board can be invoked at all. I want to avoid that, and I think the minister's Bill will avoid it. Whether or not the minister's Bill was intended to avoid it, I am satisfied if it has that effect. The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) wants to have it done in an easy and cheap way for the men. He has the same faith in the board that I have. The minister's Bill does not require them to go through the form of dickering with the company, wondering whether they are going to be promoted or interfered with in their run or anything of that kind according to how they deal with this matter. He leaves everybody free and the board decides the manner in which the compensation will be made, always provided that the men and the company do not ajgree. As the hon. member for Kings-Albert (Mr. Fowler) says, there is nothing here to prevent the men and the company agreeing. The minister's Bill requires that the order allowing the removal of the terminal shall prescribe some way in which the men shall be compensated. It does not say that the board shall only fix the amount of compensation to be given. Does the hon.
Mr. GRAHAM.
member for South Renfrew think that the board will value every man's property who may be affected by the moving of the terminal? He knows that the board would not do that, that they would appoint someone to do this or direct a certain way in which it should be done. I said incidentally that if there were many concerned a county judge could be called on, perhaps, as he would be called on to fix damages for loss of property. But that is not necessarily done and the board is simply to prescribe the way in which it shall be settled. If we all trust the board as we say we do we can leave it to them to devise the cheapest and best way to compensate the men for any loss they may have sustained.

The hon. member has
confirmed my argument in every detail and he has proved my case better than I could on account of my lack of legal knowledge. What I objected to and what he ran away from is the fact that the board would select a county judge.
I did not say that.

I am glad he took that back, it makes it better. That is the objection I took to his remarks. The board are the tribunal who can arrive at a solution of this matter in the quickest and most inexpensive manner. What I did object to was if he was going to send it to the county court judge. Then you would hardly know where it might end and expense entailed in that kind of proceeding would be altogether beyond what the minister deems proper. I am glad that my hon. friend has made my argument so clear.

Did it

There seems to be another phase of this question besides the case of the railway men. In my own constituency a railway came into a district and the fact that the railway divisional point was there, built up a town, business men came in there and invested money, they in-stahed an electric plant, and had a prosperous little town. They had a theatre and three or four churches. While the Bill protects the rariway men, which I am quite satisfied is right, at the same time if a railway company can move its terminals away from a town of that kind it is not only the railway employee who is injured but all the business men who had come into that town and invested money there. The question arises in my mind how far a railway company should be allowed to move its terminals from point to point and whether the permission of the Railway Commission is sufficient to protect the public in general I think there should be .some provision by which a man who goes into that town grows up with it, invests his money in it! perhaps employs a few hundred men, per-naps builds homes for the railway employees, should be safeguarded. If the railway terminal is removed and the railway employees have to leave the town, his business and property are depreciated, and his electric plant is not worth two cents on the dollar. To my mind this is a very big question and there ought to be some safeguard in the interests of the

men who have their money invested in such towns.

I wish to emphasize
what my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) has said. I am entirely in accord with the principle of the Bill which I think is along proper lines. To my mind it is very moderate in its terms, and not more than just. There is no doubt that railway companies sometimes find it necessary to move their terminals. Perhaps in large centres, like Toronto or London, the railway men would not have the same serious objection to move, because the property they hold might not depreciate in value to any great extent. It is in the small towns or villages which have been practically created by railways that the removal of the terminal is felt, and, as the hon. member for Selkirk has said, the public in general suffer. I have in mind a town which was created by the railway, and many other businesses have been built up there. Men have invested their all in the town and if the railway company were to move their terminal, they would practically move the town, as there is nothing else to keep business gp-ing on. The Bill as it stands provides that permission must be obtained by the railway company from the Railway Board to move their terminal, and I do not think there is any danger of the Railway Commission allowing a railway company to do so where it would destroy the whole town apart from the effect it would have on the railway men themselves. As I have already said, I am entirely in accord with the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, with the hon. member for Brock-ville, who declared that he had been employed on a railway, I may say that I have been all my life mixed up with that class of population. I must at first congratulate the Minister of Railways for having introduced the present Bill, with respect to clause 2. The county Which I have the honour to represent has also a section of railway, which employs from 250 to 300 men. It is true that it belongs to the Government, but I hope that the principle on the eve of being adopted by the companies be applied to all the Government system.
There is, however, one theory I cannot approve, and that is the increase of the salary of the chairman of the Railway Board. It appears to me that, since a few years, there is something like a race after higher salaries, especially among those who are already very well paid.
In 1906, the law had fixed the salary of the president of that Board to $10,000, and that of the other members of the same Board-because, then, there were only three Mr. BRADBURY.
-at $8,000 a year. That was already a very reasonable and very snug salary. However, two years later, in 1908, the law was amended, and, without considering the salary of the president, that of the vicepresident was raised to $9,000, and the number of commissioners was increased by the nomination of three others with a salary of $8,000 each. To-day, by a new clause, the salary of the president of the Board is raised to $12,500.
Well, I do not think that those gentlemen can show the amount of work that could justify such salaries. I have worked myself during ten years for $400 a year, and I am sure that I then worked a good deal harder than those gentlemen.
It is true that these gentlemen are recruited among the legal profession, and as the great majority in this House belongs to that profession they take good care of themselves; but, among the working classes, where life is so hard and so besought with difficulties, I am sure that protestations are heard on all sides against that constant increase of salaries in favour of a few privileged who are already too well paid.
I stand ready to support an amendment cancelling that clause.

Was it because he did not speak loud enough, or because my seat is so far that I cannot hear very well, I am at a loss to know.
As regards the salary of the President of the Board and of the Railway Commissioners, I was saying that I think those salaries are already too high, and I cannot

see the necessity of giving another increase of $2,500 to the President of the Board.
It is certain that those gentlemen are not giving, for every day, an hour of steady work.
I heard last night the member for Montcalm call attention to the fact that the members of this House are not paid as they should be. He was certainly right, because those among us -Who can work are -working ten times as much as each of those Commissioners. And, still; we only get $2,500. It is true that our salary is dignified by being called an indemnity; but, still, we are spending here our time, our energy, and even our money, all for that pitance of $2,500.
I cannot see why the members of that Board should not be satisfied with the salary they get to-day.
There is another thing I notice in the composition of that Board. There are actually six Commissioners, and only one of them is a Ffench-'Canadien, and I am not aware that the five others understand French. I do not even know if the secretary of the Board speaks French.

I beg pardon to my hon. friend, but I must inform him that there are two secretaries, one of whom is Mr. Primeau, of Montreal, whose language is French. He has been appointed at the time that the hon. member for Renfrew (Mr. Graham) was Minister of Railways.

Another commissioner
was lately appointed, and there could not have been a better occasion to render justice to our compatriots. I hope that, at the next opportunity, justice will be given to our French-Canadian compatriots.

I have the greatest
esteem for the hon. member for Rimouski, but I believe my duty is not to let pass the affirmation he has made that the members of the Railway Board were scarcely working an hour a day. It would certainly be unfortunate to let our people remain under such an erroneous impression. I may say to the hon. member that, in my quality of jurist, I have often had to plead before that Board, and I can assure him that the Board works a good deal longer than an hour a day.
There is not a member of this House who will believe what he says. He is speaking of something which he does not know. The Commissioners are working as hard as they can. JTiere is an enormous business to handle, and their responsibility is considerable. The congratulations tendered to the preceding Government, for having created that Board, were certainly well deserved. The Board has to decide questions of public interest which present an extraordinary importance. For instance, the Board regulates the rates which are being imposed on the public by great corporations. It is then extremely important that there should be there men eminently qualified. This House has had the occasion to hear both leaders on the two sides express themselves as being perfectly satisfied, not only with the present Board, but with the Board constituted by the preceding administration.
If we consider that those Commissioners are giving all their time to their work, and that they were earning formerly from $20,000 to $25,000 a year at the time they were practising their profession, it would be unfair not to pay reasonably the enormous services they are rendering to the country. I desire to make my attitude perfectly clear on that question.

For the first time, I
entirely agree with the hon. Postmaster General. However, the opinion I desire to* express on that measure is entirely of a personal nature, and does not bind any one-but myself.
If the hon. member for Rimouski was following the discussions of the Railway Board, he would realize that we have there the most important tribunal to be found in Canada. The constitution of that Board has been by far the most important act of which the preceding Government has the responsibility.
Formerly, the contests which arose between the citizen of several provinces, living in cities, villages and parishes crossed by our system of railways, were relevant of a committee of the Privy Council composed of three members, who were the Minister of Railways and two of his colleagues. That committee would sit when it had time.
As my hon. friend of Rimouski is aware, ministers are very busy. It is not possible, for the ministers, to manage the affairs of a country like Canada, without giving all their time to their official functions. The costs incurred by those litigations and the claims submitted to the committee were exorbitant.
Numerous complaints could be heard on all sides. It was then that the preceding Government saw fit-following here the example of the United States government, that had created the Interstate Commission-to create our Railway Board. In all parts of the country, the creation of that Board was hailed with joy, not only by the great companies, but especially, and above all, by the farmers, because the most humble among them, be they from the county of Rouville or that of Rimouski, may bring their claims before that Board, not at Ottawa, where the old committee of the Privy Council was sitting exclusively, but in the very localities where the Board goes . to hold its inquiries and where it renders its decisions almost " ins tan ter," reducing thus to a considerable extent the costs of litigation.
The present Board is now composed of

six commissioners, and the hon. member for Rimouski is surprised at seeing only one of French language. There are two secretaries, of whom one is French, Mr. Eugene Primeau, a young and distinguished lawyer, who was formerly in copartnership with the Secretary of State (Mr. Co-derre). Mr. Primeau was appointed by the preceding administration at the time that my bon. friend for Renfrew was Minister of Railways.
The hon. member for Rimouski can go to Mr. Primeau, and he will receive entire satisfaction; all documents and proceedings are printed in French, and I do mot know that anybody in the Province of Quebec has had so far cause for complaint as regards the French language.
Then, the hon. member takes issue about there being only one commissioner whosa language is French. It is Mr. Bernier, an ex-minister, who is vice-president of the Board. If my hom. friend takes into account, the fact that Canada is composed of nine provinces, and that the development of the railways goes on especially in the new provinces of the West, he will realize that, after all, we have our due proportion in the composition of that tribunal. At all events-

Would the minister
explain the effect of this Bill?

This Bill provides for
extending the time for exercising the right granted by the original Act of 1908 to persons domiciled in Canada who served with the British forces in South Africa in 18991902. I might re.pl iy by asking why should I make it December instead of October?
December is the end of the year

We want to get to the end of this thing, if we can. How many of these rights are still outstanding?

Somewhere between
200 and 300. About 53, I think, have surrendered. But these will be in^ a position to make their location if they chose to do so.

arisen in the case of those rights that are scheduled under the two previous extensions? In certain cases scrip was lost and there was a schedule attached. Has any complication arisen in such cases?
None that I have heard of. My hon. friend from Edmonton will know why they were specially reserved.

I think that is the
view generally entertained-that this extension should be the last; and I am prepared to promise, that, so far as I am concerned, there shall be no further extension.

I had occasion to remark before that there has been a very unfortunate opportunity for speculation arising out of the several extensions. I entirely agree with
what has been said by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). On motion of the Hon. L. P. Pelletier (Postmaster General) House went into Committee on the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient, in connection with Bill No. 188, now before this House, intituled : f an Act to provide for more advantageous telegraph communication between Canada, the United Kingdom and other parts of the British Empire, to authorize the Government of Canada, if it deems it to be in the public interest, and under the circumstances and conditions set forth in the agreement in the schedule to the said Bill, to purchase the stations, apparatus, equipment and licenses mentioned in the said agreement.-Mir.' Pelletier.
(Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)

In view of the fact that the Marconi system has been in successful operation in Canada, why does the Postmaster General discard it and inaugurate this Poulsen system? Has the science of wireless telegraphy reached such a stage that where two systems are used there is no danger of one system intercepting the messages of another.

Nothing in this Bill
prevents the Marconi from doing business and being a competitor with this company. The only thing this Bill does is to provide for a new competitor and that competitor receives no privilege, no subsidy, and no monopoly. It is simply a question of having a competitor who will bring down the prices of transmission.

The minister has
not answered my question as to whether the science of wireless telegraphy has reached such a condition that there is no danger of one system breaking into the other and thus preventing secrecy. If there is any danger, why does the minister encourage this new system?

Clause 15 of the
schedule to the Bill reads:
The syndicate declares that it has no objection to the proximity of other wireless stations and guarantees that no other stations or systems will interfere with its continuous night and day operation.

That is what the
promoters of every new proposition would claim whether it worked out in that way or not. Has my hon. friend made the independent inquiry, and if so, with what results?

I am informed that
probably some wireless companies would be interfered with if another wireless company had a station within a radius of ten or twelve miles of its station, and that is one of the reasons why this Ocean Telegraph Board is created, as one of his duties to say where these stations shall be located in order to protect the public and existing companies against possible interference. Under the existing law any company can operate in Canada, and until this Bill is passed there is no law to prevent any cable or wireless company establishing its business in Canada after getting incorporation.
That this resolution be referred to the Committee of the Whole which w considers Bill No. 188.	*
Motion agreed to.
